newsitem.title: CHINA: China says cannot open up telecommunications market.
newsitem.headline: China says cannot open up telecommunications market.

text.p: China said that it would not open its telecommunications market fully to foreign companies anytime soon since its industry was too immature, a move that could further delay its entry into the World Trade Organisation.

In a statement carried on Saturday by the official Xinhua news agency, Minister of Posts and Telecommunications Wu Jichuan was quoted making the remark to Sir Leon Brittan, Vice President of the executive body of the European Union.
Brittan was in China last month leading a delegation of European telecommunications companies and trying to accelerate China's entry into the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
Barriers to foreign companies entering China's telecommunications market were among the obstacles Beijing faced in its drive to join the world trade body.

China does not permit foreign companies to operate telecommunications networks in its domestic market. It has allowed foreign firms to sell equipment to China but it has demanded local manufacturing and transfer of technology.
China's telecommunications market has been expanding at a rapid pace.
Industry specialists estimate China will add 10 million telephone lines in 1996, bringing the total to more than 60 million by the end of the year.
It is also installing increasingly advanced equipment to modernise its telecommunications services.
Wu was quoted as saying that conditions for a fully open market were not yet mature because China's telecommunications growth relied on preferential government policies.
Unbalanced development in favour of the eastern coastal areas was another problem blocking greater participation by foreign companies, he said without elaborating.
Wu also said that the lack of separation between the telecommunications and postal services was a barrier as the two sectors now subsidise each other, according to Xinhua.
Industry officials said, however, that telecommunications services are highly profitable overall while the postal service requires government subsidies.
